title: Differentiable Lifting for Topological Neural Networks
claim: The best design choice (structure type or construction method) flips across datasets, so no single fixed choice is reliably best.
layout: 2 side-by-side grouped bar charts, left-to-right, bold keyword in each title
description: Two side-by-side grouped bar charts with a shared blue/orange palette on a light background. The left panel is titled 'Choice of domain is data-dependent' (domain in bold) and compares Simplicial (blue) with Hypergraph (orange) accuracy on Empire and Cora. Simplicial wins on Empire, at about 89 against 81. Hypergraph wins on Cora, at about 89 against 82. The right panel is titled 'Choice of lifting is data-dependent' and compares k-hop (blue) with k-nn (orange) on Cora and Wisconsin. k-hop wins on Cora, at about 86 against 74. k-nn wins on Wisconsin, at about 80 against 69, and k-hop has a large error bar there. The y-axis shows accuracy in percent, and the legends sit inside the plots. The eye goes first to the crossing bar heights, which show the reversal of rankings between datasets.
caption: [Left] Lifting to different domains can lead to disparate performances. Accuracies taken from the best TNNs in [ref]. [Right] Performances of liftings to the same domain (hypergraph) vary greatly. Values taken from [ref].
abstract: Topological neural networks (TNNs) enable leveraging high-order structures on graphs (e.g., cycles and cliques) to boost the expressive power of message-passing neural networks. In turn, however, these structures are typically identified a priori through an unsupervised graph lifting operation. Notwithstanding, this choice is crucial and may have a drastic impact on a TNN's performance on downstream tasks. To circumvent this issue, we propose $\partial$lift (DiffLift), a general framework for learning graph liftings to hypergraphs and cellular- and simplicial complexes in an end-to-end fashion. In particular, our approach leverages learned vertex-level latent representations to identify and parameterize distributions over candidate higher-order cells for inclusion. This results in a scalable model which can be readily integrated into any TNN. Our experiments show that $\partial$lift outperforms existing lifting methods on multiple benchmarks for graph and node classification across different TNN architectures. Notably, our approach leads to gains of up to 45% over static liftings, including both connectivity- and feature-based ones.
